newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New NATO-Russia council at heart of pact.
newsitem.headline: New NATO-Russia council at heart of pact.

text.p: NATO's new security deal with Russia has as its central plank a new NATO-Russia permanent joint council.
The Council, based at NATO's Brussels headquarters, will meet twice a year at the level of both foreign and defence ministers and once a month at the level of ambassadors.
The agreement was announced on Wednesday after months of tough negotiations between alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

Russia will post a permanent ambassador to the council, which will also be equipped with its own secretariat, and will exchange military liaison officers at different levels of the alliance's command structures.

The Council will have a tripartite chairmanship, shared by NATO countries, Russia and the Secretary-General. It can be convened more often if requested by one side and virtually any security issue can be raised.

The NATO-Russia accord, designed to inaugurate a new era of cooperation between the old Cold War enemies and answer Russian worries over the alliance's planned expansion eastwards, is entitled "Founding Act on Mutual Relations, Cooperation and Security between NATO and the Russian Federation".

The "Act" contains five chapters. In Chapter One, both sides commit themselves to work for the benefit of good relations. Russia pledges to continue its reform process and NATO offers to review its strategic doctrine which defines its defence posture.
Chapter Two deals with general principles of cooperation and restates the right of every state to choose its own security arrangements.
Chapter Three deals with the creation of the joint Council, and Chapter Four lists possible future areas of cooperation, such as peacekeeping operations.
Chapter Five deals with the military consequences of NATO's planned enlargement into former communist eastern Europe, and was the issue which proved most difficult to negotiate.

NATO has restated its commitment not to place nuclear weapons or foreign troops on the territories of new members, but has not renounced its right to do so. NATO also made a general commitment to further reduce conventional forces under the Conventional Forces in Europe treaty without tying the hands of negotiators in Vienna.

The alliance also offered not to use the military facilities of the now-defunct Warsaw Pact, while insisting it was the sovereign right of any country to upgrade military installations, such as airfields, as it felt fit.
